newsitem.title: UK: Adams sees room for hope on N.Ireland.
newsitem.headline: Adams sees room for hope on N.Ireland.

text.p: Sinn Fein leader Gerry Adams, speaking exactly one year after the IRA ended its ceasefire, urged Prime Minister John Major on Sunday to let his party back into Northern Irish peace talks before the British election.

The government insisted its terms for Sinn Fein's re-entry into the talks -- an unequivocal Irish Republican Army (IRA ) ceasefire -- had not changed but conceded a meeting might still prove possible.
"Any meeting before that would not be totally ruled out but would depend on the situation on the ground," said a spokesman for the government's Northern Ireland Office.
If attacks, such as those on security forces in Northern Ireland in recent weeks, continued, no meeting would be agreed before the election, which must be held by May 22.

Adams earlier hinted there might be room for progress in the stalled peace process before the British election, even though recent comments by the IRA, Sinn Fein's military wing, had cast doubt on any hope of movement by then.

Speaking on the first anniversary of the IRA's resumption of violence in its drive to end British rule in Northern Ireland, Adams urged Major to grasp for peace now rather than sit it out until the political campaigning is over.
"I don't think we should have to wait until after the British election," Adams said on BBC television.
"Even in the teeth of an election, I think it's possible if Mr Major has the political will for us to get together...to find out some way of bridging the gap," he said.
A huge bomb blast that killed two men at London's Canary Wharf business complex last February 9 heralded the IRA's return to war and threw the Anglo-Irish peace process into utter chaos.
But if Major found the courage to invite Sinn Fein representatives back for talks with the British government now, the peace process "can be moved forward", said Adams.
"Why can't that be done today or tomorrow or the next day?"
Major has barred Sinn Fein from the peace talks until the IRA reinstates its ceasefire, something IRA officials have all but ruled out until after the election.

The IRA, which seeks to end British rule of the province, has bombed security targets in Northern Ireland several times every week this year to back its demand that Sinn Fein be invited to Belfast peace talks.
In London, mourners congregated in a city centre church to honour the victims of the Canary Wharf bombing. Apart from the two men who died in the blast, hundreds saw their homes wrecked.

"The purpose of the service is to pray that people in all places be committed to reconciliation and peace, so that the seeds of national arrogance, intolerance, prejudice and fear, which so easily grow into the horror of violence, can never be sown again in our lands," Father Adrian Walker told BBC radio.
